comment.value:
This paper presents PhysDrive, a novel multimodal dataset for contactless in-vehicle physiological monitoring, which reviewers agreed fills an important gap in the field. The dataset integrates RGB, NIR, and mmWave radar sensing with six ground-truth physiological signals, collected from 48 participants across diverse real-world driving conditions. Reviewers praised the dataset’s scale, richness, and practical applicability, highlighting that it captures variations in lighting, vehicle types, road conditions, and driver movements (Reviewer 3DEa; Reviewer Przk). The benchmarking results using multiple deep learning and signal-processing methods were commended for establishing solid baselines and demonstrating both the strengths and challenges of different sensing modalities, with mmWave showing strong promise in robustness (Reviewer 3DEa). Reviewer NnJv further emphasized the seamless integration with the rPPG-Toolbox and the breadth of experimental design, which positions PhysDrive as a highly valuable and representative resource for advancing research in remote physiological sensing. Collectively, the reviewers considered the work to be technically solid, impactful, and an important step toward developing practical driver monitoring solutions.

At the same time, reviewers identified several weaknesses that should be noted. Reviewer 3DEa pointed out issues with data collection (e.g., steering wheel occlusions, radar placement, and limited discussion of NIR samples) and experimental limitations, such as the absence of multimodal fusion and the choice of training datasets for cross-dataset evaluation. Reviewer Przk also highlighted the need for clearer descriptions of signal integrity validation, rationale for method selection in different tables, inclusion of statistical measures (e.g., standard error, MACC, SNR), and further benchmarking with more recent methods and challenging datasets. Reviewer NnJv raised concerns about computational efficiency for real-time driving applications, tolerance of time drift in physiological signals, lack of scenarios for low SpO₂ evaluation, and limited discussion of cross-domain generalization. Importantly, NnJv also flagged that all participants were East Asian, raising potential concerns about fairness and generalizability across diverse skin tones and physiological characteristics. Despite these limitations, the consensus is that the contributions substantially outweigh the shortcomings, and PhysDrive provides a timely, well-executed, and impactful resource for the community.

It is quite an interesting proposal. Following your suggestion, we test on PhysDrive using FactorizePhys and PhysNet, which were trained on iBVP and PURE datasets. We compare HR extracted from the BVP output by the model with HR extracted from the ground-truth ECG.

| Method         | Train Set | Metrics | All   |
|----------------|-----------|---------|-------|
| PhysNet        | iBVP      | MAE     | 19.32 |
|                |           | RMSE    | 23.09 |
|                |           | SD      | 16.24 |
|                |           | P       | 0     |
|                | PURE      | MAE     | 19.32 |
|                |           | RMSE    | 23.25 |
|                |           | SD      | 16.28 |
|                |           | P       | -0.02 |
| FactorizePhys  | iBVP      | MAE     | 20.6  |
|                |           | RMSE    | 24.15 |
|                |           | SD      | 14.36 |
|                |           | P       | 0.02  |
|                | PURE      | MAE     | 20.92 |
|                |           | RMSE    | 24.44 |
|                |           | SD      | 14.67 |
|                |           | P       | 0.01  |

The results indicate that both models, regardless of their pre-training dataset, exhibit significantly larger errors. We also evaluate the performance at noon, when the lighting is more stable and most models performed better, and find the result is close to those obtained from the full dataset. Combining with previous findings, we argue that HR extracted from ECG signals may not be suitable for training or evaluating current video-based rPPG methods. However, we also believe that these conclusions still require further verification through additional experiments with more datasets. The underlying reasons for these findings warrant further exploration in the future.

Thank you for providing greater insights on the suggested investigation. 

**"We also attempted to fit the HR from ECG using PhysNet and FactorizePhys with RGB video. However, during intra-dataset evaluation, the performance of this model was inferior to previous results based on BVP."**

Yes, this is very much expected. rPPG follows the similar optical sensing principle as that of PPG, and this explains the inferior results when ECG was used to fit the models. What could be instead attempted is evaluating the models trained on BVP of other datasets (e.g. PURE, iBVP, etc.), and when evaluating on PhysDrive, HR from ECG can be used - to see if the models perform better. Although, it is not must to be responded here, this assessment may further help delineating whether the drop in performance is owing to erroneous ground-truth BVP-based HR or if it is a fundamental limitation of existing rPPG methods.

**1. Is the ground-truth HR used for evaluating RGB and NIR sensing methods derived from ground-truth BVP, and the ground-truth HR for evaluating mmWave methods derived from ECG? If this is the case, then it may be worth checking the agreement between ground-truth HR derived from reference BVP and ECG signals. It could be possible that owing to noisy BVP signals in challenging conditions, the derived ground-truth HR gets erroeneous leading to the peformance differences that are observed. Consistently validating using more reliable ground-truth HR may offer fair comparison between different remote sensing modalities.**

Thank you for your careful observations and insights on the results. We first would like to clarify that, as mentioned earlier, we tried our best to conduct data cleaning on all signals (BVP, ECG, RESP) prior to the experiment to remove unreliable data caused by device issues during acquisition. We also aimed to minimize the impact of environmental noise and physical motions through filtering and detrending operations. 

Theoretically, the ECG signal should provide higher-quality data than the BVP signal, particularly due to the effects of dynamic illumination and hand movements during BVP collection in this experiment. Therefore, we performed a consistency check on the HR extracted from BVP and ECG signals, using the HR calculation method described in our open-source code. 

| Metrics | E.M. &D. | Noon  | Night | R.&C. |
|---------|----------|-------|--------|-------|
| **MAE**     | 3.38     | 2.78  | 3.20   | 2.35  |
| **RMSE**    | 4.22     | 4.16  | 4.19   | 3.10  |
| **STD**     | 3.34     | 3.13  | 3.25   | 2.62  |
| **P**       | 0.88     | 0.84  | 0.80   | 0.85  |


Our results indicate differences in HR between the ECG and BVP signals, especially under varying lighting conditions. We suppose these discrepancies arise, on the one hand, because the optical measurement principle of BVP/PPG is sensitive to ambient light; on the other, more hand and body motions in driving affect device stability and signal quality. Despite our best efforts to eliminate these effects during the pre-experiment equipment installation and post-experiment data cleaning, they are unavoidable in our experimental setting. We also attempted to fit the HR from ECG using PhysNet and FactorizePhys with RGB video. However, during intra-dataset evaluation, the performance of this model was inferior to previous results based on BVP.

| Method            | MAE   | RMSE  | SD     | P    |
|-------------------|-------|-------|--------|------|
| **PhysNet**           | 15.87 | 19.32 | 16.09  | 0.08 |
| **FactorizePhys**     | 11.76 | 14.27 | 14.18  | 0.14 |


In summary, there are differences in HR between BVP and ECG. Nonetheless, using ECG for video-based HR measurements does not appear to be a viable option. The underlying reasons warrant further discussion, potentially linked to the differing principles by which these signals reflect cardiac activity. We will explore the results of the cross-modal comparison further in the final version according to this finding. However, since the measurement principles and differences between ECG and BVP/PPG are not the primary focus of this paper, we encourage future research to investigate this aspect further.

As shown in the PhysDriveLoader.py in the rPPG-toolbox, the dissimilarity-based data quality assessment method we used calls the ppg_quality interface in NeuroKit2 [1], which provides two quality measurement methods (templatematch [2], disimilarity [3]). Please refer to this source code for our implementation details.

[1] Makowski, D., Pham, T., Lau, Z. J., Brammer, J. C., Lespinasse, F., Pham, H., ... & Chen, S. A. (2021). NeuroKit2: A Python toolbox for neurophysiological signal processing. Behavior research methods, 53(4), 1689-1696.

[2] Orphanidou, C., Bonnici, T., Charlton, P., Clifton, D., Vallance, D., & Tarassenko, L. (2014). Signal-quality indices for the electrocardiogram and photoplethysmogram: Derivation and applications to wireless monitoring. IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics, 19(3), 832-838.

[3] Sabeti, E., Reamaroon, N., Mathis, M., Gryak, J., Sjoding, M., & Najarian, K. (2019). Signal quality measure for pulsatile physiological signals using morphological features: Applications in reliability measure for pulse oximetry. Informatics in medicine unlocked, 16, 100222.

**2. Providing pretrained weights of the benchmarking methods is recommended for reproducibility. These couldn't be spotted in the shared code and data.**

We appreciate your suggestion. Currently, we are reorganizing the experimental process data and preparing the necessary ethical and legal materials for the upcoming dataset release. Once the experimental data is collected, we will release the pretrained weights of the baselines. Please follow updates on the GitHub site for the PhysDrive and rPPG-toolbox.

Our purpose of this sentence is to clarify that, since both PURE and PhysDrive lack a specific experimental design for SpO2 estimation and their SpO2 distributions are limited, we cannot conduct cross-dataset evaluation between them. Thank you for your valuable comments. We appreciate your observation regarding the radar position issue and the potential occlusion caused by the steering wheel during rotation. Below, we address these concerns in detail:

1. We would like to clarify that, our millimeter-wave radar signal is not occluded in most cases. Our placement ensures that only when the control panel on the steering wheel is directly in front of the radar during the steering process, full occlusion appears. 

2. Steering Wheel's Geometry:  The steering wheel’s geometry allows radar signals to penetrate through its gaps, as it is not a seamless, solid surface that fully blocks radar transmission.

3. Signal Diffraction and Reflection:  The mmWave radar’s wide-angle coverage (over 120°) and resilience to obstructions ensure that temporary occlusions, such as the steering wheel, have minimal impact on signal quality. Diffraction and reflection mechanisms, combined with rich multipath effects in the cabin, enable the radar to bypass such obstructions effectively [1].

4. Temporal Data Analysis: As the vital sign is a time-series data, which needs to anlayze across the time window, like 10 seconds in our setting for both respitory and heartbeat signals. This extended time window allows the radar to aggregate sufficient data points, mitigating the impact of short-term occlusions and ensuring reliable monitoring.

Since we did not record the driver's driving activities (e.g., side cameras) in this work, we were unable to precisely extract and analyze the impact of steering process. We are looking forward to future work to conduct more tailored experimental design and research on this phenomenon.

[1]: BSENSE: In-vehicle Child Detection and Vital Sign Monitoring with a Single mmWave Radar and Synthetic Reflectors [ACM SenSys'24]

**1. During data collection, the steering wheel may cover part of the facial areas. Will this influence the rPPG signal measurement? Do authors have other options to place such cameras?**

Before the experiment, we tested various placements of cameras and radars on three vehicle types to ensure stability and driver visibility. Cameras on A0 and B segment vehicles were unobstructed. However, the optimal camera placement on the segment-C SUV did obscure a small area of the driver's chin by the steering wheel (see Figure 2 (e)). We believe this does not significantly affect rPPG measurement, as previous studies indicate the chin area has lower signal quality and is typically not included as a region of interest (ROI) [1,2]. A performance comparison across vehicle types is shown in Table A, demonstrating that the evaluation effect on the segment-C SUV did not significantly degrade compared to the other two types.

**5. PPG is often used for waveform regression. However, in line 274, …, so ECG is not a good option to work as the GT in the rPPG model training.**

For mmWave methods, we recover ECG signals, while Video-based monitoring focuses on BVP signals. The principle of mmWave-based measurement indicates the best fitting option is Seismocardiography (SCG), while it is sensitive to body motion and inapplicable for collection in driving. Compared with BVP/PPG, the time drift between ECG and SCG is smaller due to the pulse transit time. Meanwhile, BVP/PPG waveforms are smooth and lack precise cardiac-cycle features. Recovery ECG with mmWave is also a widely used setting in previous studies [4]. Therefore, we believe ECG is a better alternative for mmWave methods than BVP/PPG. 

[4] Ren, W., Cao, J., Yi, H., Hou, K., Hu, M., Wang, J., & Qi, F. (2024). Noncontact Multipoint Vital Sign Monitoring With mmWave MIMO Radar. IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques.

The main purpose of Table 4 is to compare the modes and analyze the performance of mmWave methods in different scenarios. Therefore, we only select the two baselines with the best performance in RGB and NIR as reference, which are mainly used for comparison with mmWave methods. We further supplement the mmWave-related baseline results as in above Table A (the complete version will be updated later).

**7. There are few results about NIR modality, which lacks comparison with RGB modality.**

Thanks for your suggestion. However, there are only a few open-sourced NIR-based methods. We tried our best to reproduce some, but their performance is limited. To avoid unfair comparisons due to our implementation, we selected baselines mainly from RGB-related works while claiming NIR support in our paper. Furthermore, we added the performance of NIR-based SiNC [5] under the intra-dataset protocol.

**8. Why not choose other challenging datasets for training?**

Aligning with previous studies [6,7,8], choosing PURE and UBFC for training and testing on our dataset better illustrates the challenges posed by the nature of our dataset. We attempted to train on MMPD and test on PhysDrive, while all baselines performed poorly even under stable light sources (Noon or R.&C.). We suppose that due to the high difficulty of the training set (low signal-to-noise ratio), complicating effective training and extraction of physiological data on PhysDrive. This issue is corroborated by other studies (see Figure 4 in [5]). Compared to MMPD, PhysDrive has additional noise sources, like varying natural light and body vibrations. This complexity is also evident when comparing traditional methods that do not require learning (refer to Table II in [6]). This point deserves further investigation in future work.

MTL indicates the Multi-Task Learning. We will amend this issue in the final version.

**1. Line 194-197: Although authors mention that waveform similarity-based ... to remove the noisy data.**

The data cleaning we used follows these steps: First, if the entire signal is almost constant (e.g., 0), it is considered invalid data caused by equipment malfunction (e.g., poor contact) during the collection process, and such data is discarded from the dataset. These invalid data will be abandoned from our released dataset. Then, for other low-quality data that may affect training performance, we chose the dissimilarity-based data quality assessment, which calculates the morphological distance between each segment and the template signal to obtain a signal quality score. We set the discard threshold of 0.5 and remove around 15% data before the benchmarking. The data quality assessment code we used has been added to the rPPG-Toolbox to facilitate future work, and potential users can perform data cleaning in their own way.

**2. Choices of benchmarking methods in different evaluation is not appropriately described ... Please describe the rationale of choosing the specific ones in the paper.**

In Table 4, we evaluate the mmWave method, given that our chosen scenarios may challenge mmWave monitoring. We include only the leading RGB multi-task method from Table 3 and the NIR method from Table 2, as the NIR baseline does not support multi-tasking. Given our focus on cross-dataset comparisons for video-based methods, we did not conduct further baseline evaluations in Table 4. Acknowledging the limitations of the results in Table 4, we included additional mmWave baseline results (referenced in Table A in the response to Reviewer 3DEa).

**3. It will be highly valuable to add standard error ... can further strengthen the results.**

summary.value: This paper introduces PhysDrive, the first multimodal dataset for contactless in-vehicle physiological monitoring, designed to address the lack of comprehensive datasets for real-world driving scenarios. The dataset includes synchronized data from 48 drivers across RGB cameras, near-infrared (NIR) cameras, and mmWave radar, along with six ground-truth physiological signals (ECG, BVP, respiration, HR, RR, and SpO2). It covers diverse driving conditions such as varying lighting, driver motions, vehicle types, and road conditions. The authors provide extensive benchmarks using signal-processing and deep-learning methods, demonstrating the dataset's utility for advancing research in remote physiological measurement (RPM). Key findings highlight the strengths and limitations of different sensing modalities, with mmWave radar outperforming vision-based methods in accuracy but facing challenges with road vibrations.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The first Multimodal Dataset covers ​RGB, NIR, and mmWave radar​ for in-vehicle RPM, filling a critical gap in driver monitoring research.
2. Real-World Driving Conditions​ – Captures ​dynamic lighting, driver motions, vehicle types, and road conditions, enhancing practical applicability.
​3. Authors evaluate ​signal-processing and deep-learning methods, establishing baselines for future research.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**Data Collection Issues**
- During data collection, the steering wheel may cover part of the facial areas. Will this influence the rPPG signal measurement? Do authors have other options to place such cameras?
- The place to hold the radar may also be influenced by the steering wheel movement since the steering wheel will rotate during driving. Does this influence the radar data quality?
- What is the wavelength of the NIR camera? In addition, there is no figure showing the NIR samples in the paper.

**Experiment Issues**
- The dataset is multimodal; however, there are no multimodal fusion results, and only single-modal results are provided.
- PPG is often used for waveform regression. However, in line 274, ECG was used for waveform regression. ECG signals have different waveform morphology from PPG/rPPG signals, so ECG is not a good option to work as the GT in the rPPG model training.
- Most methods used in Table 3 (intra-dataset results) are not used in Table 4 (intra-dataset results for different scenarios), which makes the results less comprehensive.
- There are few results about NIR modality, which lacks comparison with RGB modality.
- The training set (PURE and UBFC-rPPG) for cross-dataset results in Table 5 is quite different from the PhysDrive dataset. PURE and UBFC-rPPG are quite simple datasets, which may result in low performance on the challenging PhysDrive dataset. Why not choose other challenging datasets for training?
- Vehicle types are not mentioned in the experiments. How does the vehicle type influence the performance?
- What is MTL in line 231?

* The paper is well-written and easy to follow, with appropriate use of figures and tables.

* The size of the dataset with >1500K multimodal frames (RGB, NIR and mmWave), along with the corresponding ground-truth physiological signals and metrics (HR, RR, SpO2) makes this work highly valuable.

summary.value: This paper presents PhysDrive, a novel and timely multimodal dataset for in-vehicle remote physiological measurement.  The dataset is designed to address the current lack of comprehensive, real-world resources in the field of contactless physiological sensing within automotive environments.  PhysDrive includes a diverse range of sensor modalities, as well as multiple high-fidelity physiological signals, collected from 48 participants under naturalistic driving conditions.  This level of modality integration and biometric annotation significantly enhances its value compared to existing datasets. The authors have conducted a thorough set of experiments to evaluate the dataset’s effectiveness and generalizability across different signal-processing and deep-learning methods.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.	The framework is seamlessly integrated with the rPPG-Toolbox, ensuring user-friendly access and operation. This integration ensures that users can easily apply, test, and compare the proposed methods without requiring additional configuration or external tools.
2.	The authors provide detailed descriptions of the experimental configurations, including parameter settings and evaluation procedures.  A series of well-designed experiments have been carried out to thoroughly validate the performance and effectiveness of the proposed approach under different conditions.
3.	Compared to existing driving-based datasets, the proposed dataset contains a significantly larger amount of data and covers a broader range of experimental scenarios.  These improvements make it a more suitable and representative resource for evaluating remote physiological measurement methods in real-world driving environments.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Computational efficiency appears to be an important consideration for practical applications in driving scenarios, a comparative analysis of the computational efficiency across various methods and modalities is needed.
2. The discussion on the comparison between driving and indoor scenarios is limited due to the relatively simple nature of the PURE and UBFC datasets.
3. The paper states that a maximum allowed time drift of one second is tolerated, which may introduce significant errors for high-temporal-resolution biological signals.
4. Although SpO₂ was recorded, the experiment did not include scenarios designed to induce low oxygen saturation, resulting in overly concentrated distributions.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

dataset_code_comments.value: The authors provide an open-source GitHub link.

ethical_comments.value: All 48 participants are of East Asian descent, lacking individuals with diverse skin tones and physiological characteristics, which may hinder the generalizability of the dataset.

final_justification.value: As in my comment to the rebuttal, the work presents both contributions and limitations. Therefore, I will maintain my current recommendation.

title.value: PhysDrive: A Multimodal Remote Physiological Measurement Dataset for In-vehicle Driver Monitoring

abstract.value: Robust and unobtrusive in-vehicle physiological monitoring is crucial for ensuring driving safety and user experience. While remote physiological measurement (RPM) offers a promising non-invasive solution, its translation to real-world driving scenarios is critically constrained by the scarcity of comprehensive datasets.  Existing resources are often limited in scale, modality diversity, the breadth of biometric annotations, and the range of captured conditions, thereby omitting inherent real-world challenges in driving. Here, we present PhysDrive, the first large-scale multimodal dataset for contactless in-vehicle physiological sensing with dedicated consideration of various modality settings and driving factors. PhysDrive collects data from 48 drivers, including synchronized RGB, near-infrared camera, and raw mmWave radar data, accompanied by six synchronized ground truths (ECG, BVP, Respiration, HR, RR, and SpO2). It covers a wide spectrum of naturalistic driving conditions, including driver motions, dynamic natural light, vehicle types, and road conditions. We extensively evaluate both signal‑processing and deep‑learning methods on PhysDrive, establishing a comprehensive benchmark across all modalities, and release full open‑source code with compatibility for mainstream public toolboxes. We envision PhysDrive will serve as a foundational resource and accelerate research on multimodal driver monitoring and smart‑cockpit systems.
